utterances.text: In other words, a political decision to set up the Council for National Defence was taken on the 26th of May. And as we can see from this document, on the 11th of June, the decision was -- the political decision, that is, was implemented. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the logical sequence from a political decision to the operational implementation of the decision. At that time, in the month of June, no elements existed for such an activity to be undertaken. In other words, there was a plan behind all of this. And what the goal of the plan was became clear afterwards. If I may add another thing: In order to implement this decision already in the month of June, illegal organisations such as "Slobodna Bosna" was set up, which was led by Zjakic from Stari Grad municipality, and Patriotic League which was coordinated by Sefer Halilovic, as an active JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, have you ever seen the document before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one, no. But it was a -- a matter that was of common knowledge at the time. It was a public matter in the public domain. It had already been published by the newspapers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be exhibited, unless there are objections from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there are. Can I firstly be told where this comes from. Secondly it says: "On that occasion, a declaration was adopted. And we attach it herewith." Can we have the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document comes from the same source as the previous one, namely, the MUP of the Republika Srpska, team for investigations into war crimes of Banja Luka. We don't have that declaration which is one of the documents that were appended to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, it is not a document he has seen. It's a part document. We haven't got the other part. The relevance is obviously what the declaration is. I'm afraid we object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to me, the fact that this document confirms that on Monday, 11th of June, the Council for National Defence of the SDA was set up illustrates its relevance, nothing else. A declaration about this is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the suggestion which is being made and accepted with alacrity put by the witness is that this was part and parcel of some kind of plan to do something. I'm not quite clear what. But, therefore, it seems to me that it's important that we see the whole document for what it is. In any event, as I have already said, this document is not admissible through this witness because he has never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which seems to be the sort answer to your application, Mr. Zecevic. The -- I suppose it could be marked for identification at this stage, but I will not accept it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D180 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vlaski, you are aware that those who were defending in the war or those whose wartime service was recognised as of the 18th of September, 1991; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was published in the "Official Gazette" of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know the exact date. And I don't recall. But, anyway, the authorities at that time issued this information on the -- in the "Official Gazette."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you that document. This is 1D03-1032. We still don't have a translation of this document. These are just two articles that are relevant. So I suggest that we just comment on them with the witness, because I assume that he referred to or meant that that was this document, when he said that it was published in the "Official Gazette." This is the law of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina government for 2004, with the subheading the Law on the Rights of Defenders and members of their families. In Article 1, regulates the conditions, the manner, and the procedure in order to achieve the rights for war. Disabled veterans, members of their families, the members of Sehid [phoen] families, members of the families of those killed, who died, or are missing. The families of those killed, died, the missing defenders and demobilised defenders, persons that are responsible and awarded merits for their work in the defenders and liberation war, as well as other questions from the protection of defenders and wounded war veterans.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is asked to repeat a part of his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was as follows: Did you have this regulation in mind that I just read to you when you said that you read, in the "Official Gazette," this information that the term served in the war is being recognised as of the 18th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was published. That date was published in the "Official Gazette" that I saw, and I see the same date in this law. I really didn't have any need to monitor the legislature of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994 because the facts that relate to this period are familiar from "Official Gazettes" published before, precisely for reasons that included in that law were also persons who represented the organisation of the Green Berets which was mostly formed from criminals, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here, in Article 2, that defenders are considered to be members of the army, the Croatian Defence Council, and the police or the authorised organs of internal affairs who participated in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the 18th of December [as interpreted], 1991. And then, at the end of that paragraph, it says, As well as persons who participated in the preparation for defence and in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period before the 18th of September, 1991, and who were engaged by the authorised organs. When it says here that that also refers to persons who were engaged in the period before the 18th of September, does that actually refer to the categories of persons that you mentioned before? Can you please also wait before you begin answering.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that particular "Official Gazette" that I mentioned, provided for the possibility of these categories of persons be covered and have that status before the 18th of September. These are these categories of illegal formations which were formed as of June or practically May and which already did go through preparations and internal organisation and which already had their names and weaponry. And they were the ones who implemented these actions, which were planned at the political level and carried out at the operational level by these particular formations. This was probably a consequence of some ... one of the consequences of that was the killing of the wedding guest in Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there are no objections, I would like to tender this document to be admitted and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't anticipated before, but definitely, if our friends from the Prosecution side will -- will accept that, we will -- we will have it as a part of the law library, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All very sudden. We got it today without a translation. We have never seen it before. I don't know -- that's clearly not the Gazette either. So where is the Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we downloaded this from the web site of the -- of the -- of the Government of Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is why it is not in a proper form as a Gazette. But this is it the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Inasmuch as it is accepted that this is the law - and I don't know that there's going to be any dispute as to its authenticity - it is simply a mechanical matter of getting it translated, which would happen eventually, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So can it be marked for identification then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We don't have to mark it either, do we? Hadn't we agreed that the library is a work in progress, and, at the end of exercise, counsel would jointly hand over -- lay over to the Chamber what -- what is in this basket that we call the law library?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. But this is something which just popped up like two days ago, and it wasn't -- it wasn't -- it wasn't a part of our understanding with -- with our friends from the -- from the -- from the -- from the Prosecution side. And that is why I'm just raising this issue. We are perfectly willing to add it to the law library, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to give an undertaking at this stage without seeing further as to whether we are going to agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I will move on then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Vlaski --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, Mr. Zecevic, it has been brought to my attention during the break that inasmuch as this last document, the Prosecution has reserved its position on that it may or may not eventually make its way into the law library. The safer course would be to have it marked for identification so it doesn't get -- it doesn't stray out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it should be so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D181, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago we were looking at that piece of, legislation, and one of the crucial dates was the 18th of September, 1991. If you recall, can you tell me this: Was this not the very same date on which the police reserve force was mobilised, pursuant to an order by Mr. Delimustafic back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with this, as well as with what I said earlier, that these paramilitary formations were granted the status of legitimacy under these provisions, and this is by far more important to me than what Delimustafic wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me, won't you, that it was on or around that date that the mobilisation of the reserve force of the police was declared in BH, pursuant to an order by the then-minister of the interior of the BH, Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Let us sum up. On 26th of May, 1991, a meeting was held where a political decision was taken that the Council for National Defence was to be set up. Approximately, at the same time, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were established. In the course of the summer, Muslim youths were sent for training to the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. As they came back from training, they joined the reserve -- police force of the police, and that same force was mobilised sometime in mid-September 1991. Is the time-line more or less correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me only add this: That alongside this process, the arming process took place as well. What were the financial sources? Well, some of it was from the budget and some of it was from the side -- sidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding of what you're saying is correct, in this way, a respectable armed force was created, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indicators point to that precisely. Because the option which existed under the constitution that they should be part of the Territorial Defence and the JNA was not utilised. Rather, the third option of creating a paramilitary force was chosen, and this had to be legitimised through a political action and through the adoption of relevant regulations by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, you, in the Ministry of the Interior, were confronted with numerous problems, such as the ones you related yesterday and earlier today. If I recall correctly, on the 9th of September, 1991, you came out, or, rather, the leading staff of the Serb ethnicity came out with a press release. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because our struggle against the windmills was pointless. We invested efforts in favour of professionalism and lawfulness and realised that it all came to nothing. Our attempt, through the political structures - and who else could we have turned to but to the Serb people whom we were part of? We could not seek international protection. We could not expect any sort of fair or at least civilised approach by the Bosniak Muslim leadership of the MUP. Thus, we were compelled, in a way, to let the public know about this. We could only inform them about this, because we could not get any protection from them just as we couldn't get any protection from the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show you 1D116. This is the press release of the managerial staff of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see the document now. Is this the press release you talked about a moment ago and confirmed its existence?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a press release issued by the managerial staff of Serb ethnicity of the MUP of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in this press release you pin-pointed some of the most typical cases, including yours, where you were not appointed to the post which you should have been given or which the SDS should have given based on the inter-party agreement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my case was among the cases that prompted the issuing of this press release. And there were some others which were even more drastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "more drastic," what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to unlawful conduct, which became the standard practice of a state institution and instead should have been punished. No control could be enforced, because the key positions of control were usurped by the very same individuals who took over the legislative, executive, and judicial functions all at once. I mentioned the case of Mr. Zijo Kadic, who was the chief of a centre, member of the parliament, and a presiding -- or the chief of the State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How can a member of the Serb people expect such an individual to take any measure or initiative against the practices that became very prominent? It was quite clear that there was no political will to do that. Not only that, but there was another ulterior motive which dictated precisely what -- that what was done should be done in the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P902 was shown to you yesterday. This is an intercept involving Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Karadzic, and I think it bears the date of the 16th of September. They're having a conversation about the problem which arose concerning your appointment. Do you recall that? That's P902.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when my learned friend was showing you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 4 of P902. And that's page 4 both in the Serbian and English versions. Page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic says - and in English, it's in the middle of the page. He says: "If Avdo Hebib and Hilmo would remain here, I will not. To be clear, I will not go there. I will form a separate ministry." If my understanding is correct, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic tells Mr. Karadzic that because it is impossible to honour the agreement, he would, as the last resort, form a separate ministry. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is the 16th of September, and these events happened in that very period. Throughout the year, the nine months were characterised by the very policies that I explained. It was a time-limit within which all the vital functions should have been made operational and not just for national security but for these institutions to become operational. But this deliberate obstruction, which completely bypassed the political rules, colleagues, and institutions, led us to a situation where Mr. Vitomir Zepinic, a top notch intellectual, who, to his misfortune, did not have extensive experience with the police or with criminals - he wasn't really skillful at discussing matters with criminals - well, this proved to be his disadvantage, not an advantage. It was a misfortune for us that we had to endure such relations. Whatever the case, those who are in power, once they realise they have power, they do what they will. Those of us who did not have power, had to do the little we could; and we could do basically nothing. This helplessness and desperation that led Vito into a situation where he said that he would create a separate institution, such an intellectual who advocated lawfulness in the face of individuals who only knew the tool of force and -- and the language of force, had to resort to this. I suppose I would be able to tell you enough about these relations to fill a book of memoirs. But the statement he made here best illustrates the edge to which we were pushed. On the other side, the political leadership did not have a political response to the situation. They had been fighting for something for nine months and realised that they could not win the game. They realised that their coalition partners with whom they believed they had come to terms -- with -- about something, these three peoples could only co-exist on the principle, on principle of an agreement among the three peoples. And the agreement was possible only through the mediation of the international community, because there was no goodwill on the part of these two peoples - and I'm referring basically to the political leadership, not to the individuals themselves - they did not have a voice that could be heard. Unfortunately, individuals with a criminal past took up certain positions thanks to certain conditions which prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They got a chance to do something. And what they did was the very worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you will agree with me that one of the tactics which was pervasive and particularly prominent in the Ministry of Interior was to postpone and drag the resolution of certain issues that were raised by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a part of the plan. It was not -- it didn't amount to postponing anything. Mr. Izetbegovic, as he came out of prison, already had an idea of how he was going set up a party and take over power. Clearly, the policy was to break up the existing state for the preservation of which, unfortunately, representatives of the Serb people fought. And this was confirmed by the plebescite which was aimed at preserving Yugoslavia, which was - and this is admitted by many now - tailored to fit everyone. We were supposed to catch up with the progressive world. And God knows when we will do it now, because we're still dealing with the same issues we were dealing with back in 1991 and 1992. And, for that reason, it was impossible to expect someone who already had a plan prepared -- well, the Serbs didn't have a plan. They clearly made their political view loud and clear and that was that they wanted to preserve Yugoslavia. Now, we were supposed to be given a role of a national minority, and this is something that clearly transpires from one of the conclusions of the Badinter Commission. If this was an option that we were going to be given, and if it was clear that Izetbegovic received political and international support to organise a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina - which, by the way, was never verified by any of the institutions - this particular act - which was organised in Bosnia and Herzegovina without the participation of the Serb people, and this was counter-constitutional - had never been verified by the BH organs. And by the letter of the law, it was counter-constitutional because the legislation of the BH clearly envisaged a procedure for the verification of the results. Just as the results of the 1991 census in Bosnia and Herzegovina had never been verified. In other words, everything was a travesty in that state because somebody wanted it to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "plan," I assume that if we place the -- the events from September and the whole of 1991 into context, then a part of that would be the declaration on the independence of October, which was adopted by the Assembly in violation of the constitution, the rules of procedure, and other regulations.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just now the speeding up of the political process to buy some time so that things could be completed faster. Along with the political aspect, all the other preparations were continuing to give us some kind of role that we could not accept. Now, I'm talking about the people from my ethnic group because this is where my origin is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that the European Union, in late 1991 and early 1992, joined the plan to seek a peaceful solution for the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This plan was called the Cutileiro Plan and envisaged a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three entities with separate organs, which, at the time, was believed to be the only reasonable and rational solution in order to resolve the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very well. Every event has left a thick mark on my memory. And such an event is something that I do remember very well. Also because we saw it as a chance. Finally someone did see that there was a problem there that had to be resolved adequately and in a timely fashion. However, the plan and the assistance that came from the outside was something that somebody did not need. And after all of this, we can see who did not need this. The Serbs were willing to accept such a solution. The manner and the way in which this agreement would be reached was just a question of good will, how to implement that, but, of course -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that Mr. Izetbegovic also agreed to the plan after which he withdrew his signature or his agreement from the document?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a matter that is known. Mr. Izetbegovic was never consistent in his policies. His tactics was to be unpredictable and inconsistent, and it cost the other political structures a lot, particularly the Serb political structures. If you believe the man, then that would, at the same time, be your punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he was consistent with his plan, as you said?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that he probably was. But the way in which you need to achieve a plan, you need to have different tactical manoeuvres and an approach. In order to implement this plan, he used all kinds of methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you talked about my -- talked with my learned friend about the meeting of the 11th of February, 1992, in Banja Luka. That was not a secret meeting, was it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in no way a secret meeting. I can absolutely claim that, that it was not a secret meeting of any type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that several of those who addressed the meeting talked about the need to submit the conclusions to the then-minister, Mr. Delimustafic, and to give deadlines in order to surmount certain problems. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our approach; let's reach an agreement. And we did offer the possibility for an agreement. However, trouble forced us to assemble at this meeting. Had there been any kind of plan, we would have managed to meet in this composition during a year or so that had gone by. We would probably have sat down somewhere, organised ourselves, prepared ourselves. We would have done something on some kind of political platform or would have had some other tasks to implement. Trouble forced us to meet on the 11th of February, 1991, for the first time. What does this mean, for the first time? This means that we did not have -- other than these few colleagues on this list whom I knew personally, these were all the other people that I met for the first time. And this indicates the scale of our trouble, that we didn't even have time to meet each other personally. Whose fault is that? It's the fought of our leadership. I, as the chief of the 5th Administration, was prevented from moving around as an authorised official. In order to prevent me from moving around, Minister Delimustafic, actually the deputy for -- or assistant for finances Bruno Stoic wrote an order stating that no one can go more than 5 kilometres away in any official vehicle without the permission of the minister. So I was humiliated; I had to wait at the secretary of the minister's office for her to write some kind of authorisation so that I could go on a business trip. While my colleagues, Muslims and Croats, could travel distances of 300 or 500 kilometres and didn't have to account for that to anyone. And this is why we met for the first time. And I regret that we met only then for the first time. Had we been meeting more or before, our response would probably have been more effective, and we would have had probably the possibility of having some sort of influence on any situation. But this is what -- how it all worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we please show the witness 1D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend put questions to you yesterday about this meeting, and you did give your comments on that, so I don't want to go into that again. But one of the things that was stated was the matter of the arming of the police reserve forces of Serb ethnicity. Isn't it a fact that, in 1991, the police reserves were mostly replenished by Muslims. They were mostly summoned into the reserves?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Correct. We, at the Ministry of the Interior, had, as far as I know, about 10.000 members, uniformed policemen. And those who were just employees were not police officers. And we also had a certain number of reserve forces. According to the list, which is taken as the relevant criteria in 1991 - the ratio along the ethnic lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina is known to everyone - so that structure was supposed to correspond to the ethnic structure of those employed in all the institutions. So that structure was supposed to reflect the constitution and the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina in institutions and some public enterprises as well. It -- the situation with the employees there was supposed to reflect the overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For example, in western Herzegovina, the Bosniak -- the Croats were in a -- in a majority. Then, in some other places, had you Muslims, Bosniaks, who were in a majority. So that, perhaps -- situation was not reflected right there. But precisely for that reason, at the level of the former Yugoslavia, the Serbs did constitute a majority. And the prevalent opinion in Bosnia and Herzegovina was that they were also a majority in that segment in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Nobody ever provided specific data about the ethnic structure of the cadres employed there. That organisational unit was under the control of Mr. Hilmo Selimovic, who was mentioned as few times before, who came to the ministry from a post as the director of the brewery. So they were these authentic -- authentic people who were interpreting these lists. And you can imagine the objectivity that they had when they provided their views on the protection of the constitutional order and the actual state of affairs in the government. That didn't even occur to them. They could adjust the data the they wanted to and put the stamps on that, and they were not obliged to report about that to anyone. They didn't have to report to anybody or be responsible to any kind of political structure. So, of course, this is all in the sphere of legend. They couldn't just sack people from the MUP for some frivolous reasons; I mean, it was also a social question, not just a political question. So then they refrained from that sort of revenge, but they used all sorts of more subtle methods of replenishing the staff. And this is why they thought up of this principle of the reserve composition through which they were supposed to create an armed force, a legal armed force which would be part of the ministry forces, which, if needed, could turn into a military force, because those persons who were recruited were of specialties by establishment as drawn up by Sefer Halilovic, representing the Patriotic League, because he had military training. And this is what they coordinated. They had all had coordination at the SDA level, and the National Defence Council, together with cooperation from the HDZ, because they did need an alliance in relation to Serbia. They needed an alliance with Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they were also settling their accounts through Bosnia and Herzegovina to the detriment of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to be more concise because I think we have lost track of the question here. Was it not a fact that -- to a greet degree, Muslims were mostly called to join the reserve forces of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in those areas of the public security station where the reserve forces had a Muslim minority -- majority, the MUP would provide for material and equipment to precisely those places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in the same way, in the territories of the public security stations, where the Serbs were in a majority in the reserve forces, actually no weapons or materiel or equipment was sent by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that nothing was supplied, but there is another fact which is even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another fact I am aware of. Certain assets were deliberately taken out of the centres where the Serbs had at least some form of influence or clout. This is particularly typical for state security, and this is the sector I'm most familiar with. When all the operative technology, which was by the order of Dautbasic, withdrawn from all the centres and stored in -- at one location in Sarajevo. This made it impossible for all the people out in the field to work. The official justification was that they wanted to prevent the equipment from being misused. They stored all the technology and the equipment in the head office and used it for their own purposes as they saw fit, and we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you discussed this yesterday. Let me sum up. On the one hand, the public security stations where Serbs were in the majority, materiel and technical equipment, including uniforms, were not supplied; whereas, on the other hand, what little they did have was taken away from them and taken to the Sarajevo head office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the available receipt documentation, you can see that the equipment was taken, through unlawful means and methods, away; and the individuals who were in charge of these facilities didn't have an opportunity of using them anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So some of the matters discussed at the meeting by Mr. Andrija Bilosevic, among others, who complained about the fact that did he not have any more weapons. Then there was another individual who said that they didn't have uniforms in sufficient numbers, et cetera, these were, indeed, matters which bothered the heads of public security stations and others who were represented at the meeting, and they did have an actual basis.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All these claims had a basis because they were based on the situations that prevailed in the various stations. And there was a need to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us, therefore, conclude. The requests put forth at this meeting were not aimed at additional arming of policemen of Serb ethnicity. This was merely a request for all the policemen, regardless of their ethnicity, to be fully equipped, all those who worked within the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The only logical explanation, and this is a fact, is that this was the sole objective of these requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact as well that in the February of 1992, not only did you, as members of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of Serb ethnicity, see no other way out of the situation then the formation of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. You also enjoyed the support of the European Union which had a plan of division of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the principle of the three entities. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We merely followed a line of thinking, a policy, which wanted to solve the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because neglecting or ignoring the interests of one people would lead to an enormous difficulty for Bosnia-Herzegovina. You cannot run a concern policy whilst completely ignoring the interests of one people. The international negotiations which took place and as far as the Lisbon Plan the Cutileiro Plan were concerned, they were headed in that same direction. Later on, this plan was, in a modified version of it, brokered by the international community and these were the Dayton Accords. That was the only possible political settlement. Now let me answer your question. The MUP leadership consisting of individuals of Serb ethnicity didn't have any other choice because the political tendency was for certain regions of municipalities to be set up through which authority would be established on a regional principle. These were the well-known SAO Krajinas. This was an option which was offered, and this was offered in the discussions concerning the constitutional amendments and the arrangement of the three peoples. Neither the Bosniaks nor the Croats accepted this option because it did not run in -- in their favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the last topic that I would like to discuss with you, and this was also the last topic covered with you by Ms. Korner in her direct examination, was the issue of the barricades as of the 1st of March, 1992. You repeatedly stated that in your view this was a political assassination. Now, was not one of the reasons on which you base this position of yours is the way in which the crime was committed? The wedding guest who was killed was killed in the yard of a church in Sarajevo in front of the very eyes of the wedding party.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the gravity of it all. And that's the message it sent. Had the circumstances not been such, the event would not have led to the subsequent events, if the incident itself didn't have such hallmarks. The murder of that wedding party guest was not committed because of the identity of the wedding guest -- party guest, but, rather, because of the Serb insignia, of the Serb flag. And the message was that they shouldn't be there. And then, by the same token, they shouldn't anywhere. They were not desirable in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. Now, where would this lead us, the Serbs, as a collective and let alone the individuals themselves? So should an individual merely fall flaunting a flag constitute a target for that very same reason? Should such a gesture have such drastic consequences? Is this what should befall a person who strikes a song or -- was this supposed to be the fate of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And particularly the fact that the murder was committed at the threshold of a church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It has a wider dimension if we analyse it from the political point of view. The wedding could take place in a registrar's office without any problems, but, in a church, Serbs, at Bascarsija, should they really be there? Well, the message that was sent was, You came there this once, but that was your last time you were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you confirmed that the perpetrator was identified and arrested and subsequently released. One of the eye-witnesses told us that according to the information he had, the order came directly from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, from where are you quoting? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the position of the Trial Chamber is that we are not allowed to -- to give the name of the witness. We can cite the words of the witness without disclosing the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't agree with that. The rule is you cannot -- you can put propositions to this witness; they should not be preceded by the words "Somebody has told us this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Rephrase the question, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the proposition itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information that from interviewing the person arrested, according to that, the information came directly from the office of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that particular knowledge, but all the facts, i.e., actions of the MUP officers involved, indicate that it was not done in a professional manner. The response of the persons authorised was not either professional or in accordance with the law. The individual should have been firstly arrested, and, secondly, detained. However, the person was hidden away. Evidently he had the protection of the police. And the evidence from the crime site disappeared. Only 15 years later did the BH judiciary start -- initiate a procedure against the suspect for the murder, but the trial was not completed because the various opposing factions were at logger heads surrounding this issue, and they liquidated the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I didn't hear the witness say that a perpetrator was arrested and subsequently released, and I didn't -- I can't see that in the answer he gave after you put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it must -- it must be -- my mind is tricking me. I feel I heard that he said that he was identified, arrested, and then released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you -- can you ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, sir, can you resolve this misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am more familiar with this issue than you are. This was the result of unprofessional conduct. The role of the authorised official is such that they first have to identify the perpetrator. And there was a policeman at the crime scene, and he was supposed to arrest the individual. However, the individual was hidden away and enjoyed protection. So I'm not talking about any sort of arrest taking place. The person who was the participant in the event was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that enough explanation, or should I pursue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, during the direct examination, you listed a number of individuals who were present in the Holiday Inn on the day you were there, including Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Stanisic claims that he was away in Mostar on official business on that day and that he returned to Sarajevo only late that evening. Do you allow for the possibility that you may be mistaken, your memory might be playing tricks with you that he was in Sarajevo on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me which period of time that was, or period of day. I was there in the evening hours myself, and that was when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that was late in the night?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there late in the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention that there's just one small matter I want to raise just before we rise today. It's purely administrative, and it shouldn't take more than a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... it is now 6.36. If you could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. It's 6.36 now, according to the clock and LiveNote. If you could break at about 6.55 to allow Ms. Korner to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vlaski, good day. I am Mr. Krgovic, and I'm representing Mr. Zupljanin. I'm going to put several questions to you that have to do with your testimony today and yesterday. In response to my colleague, Mr. Zecevic's question, you mentioned certain operative techniques from certain centres where a certain influence was excerpted by Serbs at the centre in Sarajevo. It's well known that the equipment used for wire-tapping was relocated from Banja Luka and transferred to the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from Banja Luka. It was a decision to pull that out of all the centres. That was it. It was not something that was done selectively. It was a general decision on the relocation of all the equipment to the centre, where control would be taken over by the line along the vertical subordination structure, under the control of these structures, from the ranks of the Muslim and Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this meeting on the 11th of February in Banja Luka, the opening by the host, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, when he spoke about the security and the materiel and financial situation, he also referred to this about these matters, which in the circumstances, making the work of the SUP more difficult. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a problem -- it was a general problem where some people were more affected by it and some less. It just varied in the details. It depended on the size, the security requirements, the security threat assessment. So these problems were in some places more pronounced and some places less pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D135, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the document of the minutes that you already had. So can you please look at page 4 in the Serbian version, and that is the place where Mr. Vlado Tutus from the Banja Luka centre -- Did you know Mr. Tutus?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he says there that, precisely for the reasons that you are talking about, says that the people from Bosanska Krajina have lost their trust in the MUP; the CSB in Banja Luka does not have a single all-terrain vehicle. And that problem did exist because people in the municipal and regional centres felt abandoned and believed that the Serbian cadres in the MUP had to do much more than they were objectively able to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an assembly of the desperate, not MUP leadership. Our cry was away of reacting. Mr. Tutus, probably as a policeman of many years standing in a town such as Banja Luka, had enough information about the mood of the people. And it was normal that those people would convey their dissatisfaction. And it was also normal that he, as an authorised person in charge of the security in a town, if he had nothing to defend it with and to carry out his regular duties -- I mean, we can see that he didn't have the adequate vehicles. Well, how can we talk about any kind of work? Were we supposed to get horses like we did in World War II to be able to go from one place to another?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the security problem was particularly pronounced in the Banja Luka area because of proximity of the war in Croatia and the events which were spilling over from Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the refugees from Croatia were the first refugees that arrived to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia, from Daruvar. They came to the Krajina area, they came to Banja Luka. And that pressure from Croatia was felt by the people, by the political leadership, and by the police because they were the ones who had resolve the numerous problems. And they were most affected by those problems, and they were the ones called upon to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, they were not equipped and didn't have enough people, and they asked for reinforcements in personnel; they asked for professional staff, which would help out. They asked for people from Croatia who had been left without work.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been thrown out of their jobs in Croatia. They didn't just lose their jobs. So what can a professional do? He is not going to go into some kind of trade that he never did in his life before. He was a policeman, and he was looking for a position in the police. On the other hand, we had the process of the employment of completely incompetent people to the police, even though we had perfectly capable policemen that were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was precisely the problem discussed by Mr. Zupljanin at this meeting. On the one hand, criminals were being employed in the police; and, on the other hand, we had professional who would be able to do the job properly, who were not being taken into service.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the plan. Employing criminals, misusing, deliberately, their abilities in order to implement objectives. That was part of the plan. Serbs could not employ the professionals that were offering themselves from Croatia. There was no room for Serbs in the reserve forces of the police either. They were not being trained; they were not being provided equipment or weapons. And so now we have some question being put here about the arming of these structures. Again, these are legitimate structures that were including the active police. This was a pronounced problem. What kind of a Serbian MUP or a Serbian conspiracy or a Serbian organisation can we be talking about? That is a joke even to mention it in this context. We were powerless there, and we were just speaking rhetorically in this way without any kind of concrete action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the second page of this document, one of the speakers is Cedo Kljajic and he's referring to the Motorolas which were obtained by MUP funds but were never placed in the MUP warehouses. Was that also part of this plan?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very familiar with this kind of dealing about the obtaining of this equipment because we did inform the public to a considerable degree about that, as for these Motorolas. And not only Motorolas; there were vehicles arriving, all kinds of things coming in. All of that was being directed at these structures. The Motorolas were taken by Mahmutovic whose superior I was for a certain period of time. And this went along that line, the SDA. I think that this, for us, at that time, was not really any kind of strange thing, but we didn't have the mechanisms to react. We didn't have any mechanisms; we didn't have any power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what Cedo Kljajic is saying, We Serbs are the only ones who are acting lawfully, as opposed to the SDA and the HDZ. This assertion of his is correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our problem because we naively believed that we could do something if acted legally. Until the last day, until the division in the MUP occurred, until this whole process began of the falling apart of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we naively believed that you could preserve. And this Assembly, this meeting of ours, and from the conclusions, it was evident that we were still trying to offer to Alija Delimustafic, as the minister, something. But that was just an illusion. We were trying to give him an opportunity for us to form a kind of Serbian MUP within the MUP so that we could at least be able to collect -- to assemble in a restaurant without having to hide -- to say, Well, we are Serbs; we could listen to each other; we could comfort each other; and then, if we have the opportunity, we could tell each -- you something; and then perhaps we could reach some sort of agreement or tell you at least something. However, the role of the police is not to reach agreements. Their job is to implement the laws. And the principle here, as they imposed on us, was, Well, let's agree whether we're going to follow the law or not. And, of course, they didn't need the laws. They had the political support and that was the way they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when the reserve forces were formed, when members of the Muslim ethnic group were recruited, then they went and they took records from the Defence Ministry, knowing whose specialities were of recruits who was -- were then mobilised. They were recruiting those had had certain specialised military knowledge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was already the plan drawn up by Sefer Halilovic on the military organisation of the SDA Party. And I am a witness who can affirm that Mr. Sefer Halilovic came to the Presidency to see Alija Izetbegovic, because, at that time, the Presidency was under the authority of my administration, at whose head I was, so we did know who was coming to the Presidency because it was our duty to provide counter-intelligence protection. However you couldn't do this in an institutional way. This was sort of privately-gained information, because this institutionalised work required work along the specific professional line. And the work had to are verified somewhere in order to enter into procedure. And so that pursuant to any kind of information on illegal actions, somebody would then need to take adequate measures because state security was supposed to work on the combatting of organised and illegal activities. As for legal activities, such as the legal activity of a political party, that was not part of the work of a security service, except in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where this was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, just a correction to the transcript, page 57. You said, I am personally a witness that he came. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I misspoke. I was informed about the fact that Mr. Sefer Halilovic came to the Presidency to see Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to break up my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This is a convenient point, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Vlaski, the -- we are about to take the adjournment for the day. Your cross-examination is still not complete, and before the Usher escorts you from the courtroom because the Court is not going to rise immediately, I would remind you of what I said yesterday about not discussing the matter with other persons. Thank you. So we would resume at 2.15 tomorrow in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first thing can I say, we can do in open session; and the second matter, I would like to go into private session for. But it's a question of tomorrow. The next witness is only arriving late tonight. We had a request last week from Mr. Zecevic to be able to interview that witness before he testifies. We suddenly, today, had a request also from Mr. Krgovic who would also like to see this witness, which is not a request we've had before. This witness, it would seem, is going to finish pretty quickly tomorrow afternoon as I understand from Mr. Krgovic. So we will not be able to go, as a result of these requests and apart from the fact that he has also got to look through documents, we won't be able to call that witness tomorrow. So there will be, I am afraid, a break at the conclusion of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Actually, the office -- your office had alerted us to the that in the note that was sent to Ms. Featherstone, when was this, on the 10th? On the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I hadn't -- I've obviously missed that one or forgot about it. So just so Your Honours are aware of that. We're now getting requests to see just about every other -- every witness we're calling between now and Easter from both counsel. So can I make it clear: We'll do our best do accommodate them, but, obviously, VWS aren't happy about witnesses being here for a very long time. And really it is incumbent upon the Defence, if they want to interview these witnesses, to make their own arrangements, rather than us having to factor in that when we bring them up here. So I'm just, as it were, putting down a marker, as somebody in my chambers would say. Your Honours, for the second matter, can I just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of February, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
